introduction-the-linear-trap.core: Simple systems fail through one broken part. Complex systems (distributed software and the organisations running them) fail through interactions, emergence and adaptation, so linear cause-and-effect thinking misleads.

first_principles.problem: Teams treat outages like a broken car part, replace 'the cause', and are surprised when different-looking failures keep coming.
truths: Complex systems have many interacting parts.
People continuously adapt to keep systems running.
derivation: Shift from Safety I to **Safety II**.
Mind the **work-as-imagined vs work-as-done** gap and the **ETTO** trade-offs.

analogy.title: A car engine vs. a city's traffic
analogy.story: An engine fault has one broken part; a traffic jam emerges from thousands of drivers' interactions.
analogy.breaks: Some incidents really are simple, but don't assume that by default.

example.title: A cascading outage
example.outcome: you think in systems, not broken parts.

check.q: Why does linear root-cause thinking fail for complex systems?
check.a: Outages emerge from interactions among many parts that each behaved reasonably, not from a single broken component.

the-fallacy-of-root-cause.core: 'Root cause' implies one broken part. In complex systems, the cause you name depends on where you stop asking, often at a person, which hides the systemic conditions. Talk about contributing factors instead.

first_principles.problem: Postmortems conclude 'root cause: human error' and recommend 'be more careful'.
truths: The stopping point of analysis is a choice.
Human error is a symptom of system design.
Naming one cause narrows the fixes.
derivation: Treat **'human error'** as a starting point, not a conclusion.
Ask **why the action made sense** at the time.

analogy.title: Blaming the last domino
analogy.story: The last domino didn't cause the fall. The whole arrangement did.
analogy.breaks: Teams still need focus, so prioritise the factors you can most influence.

example.title: 'Human error' reframed
flow: Why possible? No confirmation, prod creds on laptop
Why normal? Ops did manual fixes weekly
Fixes: tooling, guardrails, fewer manual ops
example.outcome: analysis that reaches the conditions behind errors.

check.q: Why is 'human error' a poor conclusion in an incident review?
check.a: It stops analysis at the person and hides the system conditions that made the error likely and harmful.

sidney-dekker-and-drift-into-failure.core: Dekker's 'drift into failure': organisations slide toward disaster through many small, locally reasonable decisions under pressure (skipping a check, raising a threshold), each of which normalises a little more risk until the margin is gone.

first_principles.problem: No single decision looks dangerous, yet over two years safety margins quietly erode until a catastrophic failure.
truths: Small deviations become normal when nothing bad happens.
Erosion of margins is invisible day to day.

analogy.title: Boiling a frog slowly
analogy.story: Each degree of temperature rise feels fine until it's too late.
analogy.breaks: Not every deviation is drift. Some adaptations are improvements.

example.title: A drifting alert threshold
flow: Disk fills before anyone reacts → outage

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Each change seemed sensible on its own.

example.outcome: slow erosion of safety gets noticed and reversed.

check.a: The gradual acceptance of practices that deviate from safe norms because nothing bad has happened yet.

safety-i-vs-safety-ii.core: Safety I defines safety as the absence of failures and learns mainly from incidents. Safety II defines it as the ability to succeed under varying conditions and learns from everyday work, which is mostly successful.

first_principles.problem: Studying only the rare failures ignores the 99.9% of operations where people adapt successfully.
truths: Success and failure come from the same adaptive behaviour.
Learning from success is plentiful and low-stakes.
derivation: **Safety II**: understand how things usually go right.

analogy.title: Studying only car crashes vs. studying good driving
analogy.story: You learn much more about safe driving by watching how millions of trips go well.
analogy.breaks: Safety II complements Safety I rather than replacing it; failures still need analysis.

example.title: A Safety II review
flow: Find engineers routinely pre-warm caches manually

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: An invisible safeguard is made reliable.

check.q: How does Safety II define safety?
check.a: As the ability to succeed under varying conditions, the presence of adaptive capacity rather than the absence of failures.

work-as-imagined-vs-work-as-done.core: Work-as-imagined is how procedures and runbooks say the work happens. Work-as-done is what people actually do to get results under real constraints. The gap shows where documentation, tools and assumptions are wrong.

first_principles.problem: Runbooks describe a process nobody actually follows, so in an incident the 'official' steps fail.
truths: Real conditions vary beyond what procedures foresee.
People adapt to get the job done.
Ignoring the gap leaves fragile assumptions.
derivation: **Update** procedures and tooling to match reality.

analogy.title: A recipe vs. how grandma actually cooks it
analogy.story: The written recipe says '2 cups'; grandma adjusts by feel and the dish only works her way.
analogy.breaks: Some deviations really are unsafe shortcuts, so understand them before endorsing them.

example.title: A deploy runbook gap
flow: Reality: engineers first run 3 undocumented checks

check.a: They show where procedures, tools or assumptions don't match real conditions.

the-efficiency-thoroughness-trade-off-et.core: Hollnagel's ETTO principle: people constantly trade thoroughness (checking everything) for efficiency (getting things done) because time and resources are limited. Outcomes judged in hindsight label the same trade-off 'smart' or 'reckless'.

first_principles.problem: After incidents, reviewers call skipped checks negligence, while the same shortcuts are praised as efficiency on normal days.
derivation: Make **critical checks cheap** (automation) so thoroughness costs less.
Judge decisions by **what was known then**.

analogy.title: Proofreading under a deadline
analogy.story: You skim to hit the deadline; if a typo slips through, critics call it careless, but on most days skimming was right.
analogy.breaks: Some checks must never be skipped, so make those mandatory and automated.

example.title: A skipped canary
flow: Fix: make canary 5 min and mandatory
example.outcome: systems designed so the safe path is also the fast path.

check.q: What's the best organisational response to the ETTO principle?
check.a: Make critical safety steps cheap and automatic, so people don't have to trade them away under pressure.
